entries.meaning: Janaka bows to the assembly of sages and receives every blessing, then respectfully embraces his sons-in-law, the brothers who are treasures of beauty, character and virtue. With lotus-like hands joined, he asks how he could praise Rāma: the swan of Śiva and sages’ mind-lake, sought by yogis who renounce anger, delusion, attachment and pride; the all-pervading, unseen, imperishable Brahman, consciousness and bliss, beyond attributes yet treasury of virtues; the one neither mind nor speech nor inference can know, whom the Veda describes only as ‘not this,’ unchanged through all time. By divine favour that root of all joy has become visible to Janaka’s eyes.

Janaka says Rāma has honoured him in every way and embraced him as a servant. Even ten thousand Sarasvatīs and Śeṣas writing for millions of ages could not exhaust either Janaka’s fortune or Rāma’s virtues. Trusting only that Rāma is pleased by the smallest sincere affection, he repeatedly begs one gift: may his mind never stray from Rāma’s feet. Rāma, fulfilled in himself yet nourisher of love, is pleased and courteously honours his father-in-law as he would Daśaratha, Kauśika and Vasiṣṭha. Janaka lovingly blesses Bharata, then embraces and blesses Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna as all repeatedly bow.

After repeated courtesies Raghupati departs with all his brothers. Janaka grasps Kauśika’s feet and places their dust upon his head and eyes, saying that after the supreme sage’s sight nothing seems unattainable; the fame and joy for which guardians of worlds hesitate even to hope have become easy for him, since every perfection follows the sage’s presence. He bows again and returns with blessings. The procession moves to drums, gladdening every village along the road as people feast their eyes upon Rāma, and after pure days of travel the wedding party reaches the outskirts of Ayodhyā.

Great drums, tabors, kettledrums, conches, horses, elephants, cymbals and shehnais resound. Hearing the procession approach, Ayodhyā’s people thrill and adorn their houses, markets, roads, crossroads and gates. Every lane is sprinkled with fragrance and filled with elegant designs; shops, arches, flags, banners and canopies become indescribably beautiful. Laden areca, plantain and mango stand with bakula, kadamba and tamāla trees whose lovely gem-made basins seem to touch the earth. Auspicious pitchers decorate every house, and Brahmā and the gods envy Rāma’s city.

Daśaratha’s palace shines so splendidly that even Love is enchanted. Auspicious omens, beauty, prosperity, mystic power, happiness and wealth seem to take bodies and fill every part of the house. Who would not long to see Rāma and Vaidehī? Groups of married women, each beauty scorning Love’s pleasures, assemble every auspicious article and sing like Sarasvatī in many forms. Noise and bliss beyond description fill the palace. Kauśalyā and Rāma’s other mothers forget bodily awareness in love, worship Gaṇeśa and Śiva, give abundant gifts to Brahmins, and rejoice like paupers who have obtained all four human aims.

All the mothers are so overcome with delight that their bodies weaken and their feet scarcely move. Longing to see Rāma, they eagerly prepare the welcoming rite. Sumitrā arranges auspicious music and gathers turmeric, sacred grass, curds, leaves, flowers, betel, areca nuts, rice grains, shoots, fragrant buds and tulasī sprigs. Beautiful gold pitchers look like nests fashioned by Love’s omens. The queens prepare many kinds of lamps and auspicious offerings, fill golden trays, take them in lotus hands, and advance with bodies blossoming in thrilled joy.

entries.meaning: Incense darkens the sky like a proud bank of monsoon clouds. Gods rain garlands of heavenly flowers like rows of white cranes; jewelled festoons seem rainbows drawn by Indra. Women flash into sight and hide again upon terraces like quick lightning, while celestial drums roar like clouds and petitioners become thirsty cātakas, frogs and peacocks. Fragrant sacred water falls and every city-dweller is happy. At the guru’s command Raghukula’s jewel enters the city with the rejoicing king and company, remembered together with Śiva, Girijā and Gaṇeśa, amid omens, divine flowers, drums and dancing goddesses.

Bards, heralds, performers and citizens sing Rāma’s world-renowned glory. Pure victory cries and noble Vedic voices steeped in blessing ring through all directions; instruments fill heaven and city, and the magnificently dressed guests can scarcely contain their joy. Citizens salute the king and grow happy gazing upon Rāma, offering jewels and garments with tearful eyes and thrilled bodies. Women joyfully wave lamps before the four princes. When the curtains of the graceful palanquins are opened, they rejoice at the brides; thus giving delight to all, the couples reach the royal gate, where the mothers welcome sons and brides together.

Again and again the mothers perform lamps, love and joy beyond measure, and offer countless ornaments, jewels and fabrics. Seeing all four sons with their brides, the mothers sink into supreme bliss and regard their worldly lives as fulfilled. Sītā’s companions repeatedly gaze upon her face, sing, and praise their own good fortune; gods continually shower flowers and join in song, dance and service. Sarasvatī searches every simile for the four enchanting couples but finds each entirely too small, and remains fixed upon their beauty. After Vedic and family rites, arghya and cloth pathways, the mothers escort them home.

Four naturally beautiful thrones, seemingly fashioned by Love himself, receive the four princes and princesses. The mothers wash their sacred feet and worship each auspicious bride and groom with incense, lamps, food offerings and Vedic rites, repeatedly waving lamps and fly-whisks and giving away many gifts. Their joy surpasses by hundreds of millions the happiness of a yogi finding ultimate truth, a chronically ill person gaining nectar, a lifelong pauper finding the philosopher’s stone, a blind person receiving sight, a mute receiving Sarasvatī’s speech, or a warrior winning battle. Watching the shy brides and mothers perform household customs, Rāma smiles inwardly.
